name: Neoconservatism
summary: Neoconservatism is an American variant of conservatism that arose in the 1970s among former liberals and anti-communists. It accepts a reduced but real welfare state and a qualified market economy built on growth, treats culture and religion as political concerns, and favours an assertive foreign policy that uses American power and promotes democracy abroad while distrusting world government.
scope: The American neoconservative persuasion as Britannica (Ball and Dagger) and Irving Kristol define it, from the 1970s (Kristol, Podhoretz, Glazer, Bell, Moynihan, Kirkpatrick) through the Bush-era foreign policy. It uses Kristol's own accounts, Kirkpatrick's essay that Britannica names as the neoconservative case, and Podhoretz's writing; it excludes think-tank platforms such as PNAC and non-American uses of the term.

notes: Evidence is all words: neoconservatism has no regime or party record. Searched: Kristol's essays (growth, welfare, culture, religion, foreign policy), Britannica, Kirkpatrick and Podhoretz. The sources are about foreign policy, the welfare state and culture; economy details, government structure, civil liberties, ecology, technology, gender, race and most of world policy have no stated position, so those answers are null. PNAC material was left out as an organisational platform. Britannica's own copy was read through the Wayback Machine because the site refuses scripted access. Race, ethnicity, secession and monarchy were searched for in Kristol, Britannica, Podhoretz and Kirkpatrick and by web search for Glazer and Kristol on multiculturalism; the sources say nothing on them that settles a statement, so the uncertainty rule rejects this audit on lines 5, 11, 1 and 7.
